messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Jian is a 41-year-old South Eastern Asian man who has been working as a dancer in New York City for over two decades. Married and deeply involved in his community, Jian was a relief worker in a war zone before his current occupation. His experiences there have left him with profound psychological scars that he has struggled to overcome. The traumatic event occurred late one afternoon while Jian was delivering supplies to a refugee camp in the middle of gunfire. The smell of burnt buildings and alcohol from the makeshift shelters still haunts him, especially at that same time of day when the trauma unfolded. Every time he encounters these smells, or even when it is the exact hour the event took place, Jian’s mind involuntarily replays the horrifying scenes in vivid detail. One evening, as Jian was preparing for a performance, the smell of burnt wood from a nearby bonfire triggered an overwhelming memory. He found himself transported back to that day in the war zone, feeling the same fear and helplessness he had experienced then. The sensation was so intense that he felt like he was reliving it all over again. Jian’s distress was exacerbated by the intense shame he feels every time he recalls the event, as if he is re-experiencing the violation of his own values. Jian’s negative appraisals have deepened this cycle of trauma. He has come to believe that his actions during the crisis were antithetical to who he is and that his reactions since then demonstrate poor coping abilities. These beliefs make it difficult for Jian to trust himself, which in turn heightens his anxiety whenever he encounters a trigger. The more he feels like he can't rely on himself, the more vigilant he becomes about potential triggers. This heightened vigilance has led to avoidance behaviors that have strained both his personal and professional life. At work, the smell of alcohol from fellow performers or even the time when he used to rehearse now cause him intense distress. Jian has started avoiding certain rehearsals and performances, leading to conflicts with his dance company and a significant drop in his performance quality. Jian’s wife also notices changes in his behavior. He often cancels plans at the last minute due to unexpected triggers or feels too anxious to participate fully. His avoidance of situations that might lead to these experiences has created tension within their relationship. The weight of his negative appraisals and memories has become overwhelming. Jian is now at a point where he cannot continue living this way. The constant fear and shame are taking a toll on his physical and mental health, and the strain in his marriage has reached a breaking point. He has finally decided to seek help, hoping that therapy can provide him with the tools to manage his reactions and regain control over his life. What frightens Jian most is the prospect of never feeling safe again, unable to trust himself or those around him. However, he also harbors a glimmer of hope that through treatment, he might find a way to reconcile his experiences and live without constant reminders of that harrowing day in the war zone.
